title-group.article-title: More Awards, Lower First-Prize Rates? How Award Tiers Shape Comparisons in Shenzhen’s Venture Competition

contrib-group.aff: Business School, Jiangsu Open University, 210000 Nanjing, China

abstract.p: A binary measure of success treats a venture that wins a noncash award and one that qualifies for prize money as equivalent. This study examines how that choice affects comparisons between locally registered enterprises and teams without local registration at entry in Shenzhen’s innovation and entrepreneurship competition. All 455 entries in the 2024 and 2025 industry finals were checked against the published results, 323 awards were matched to finalists, and the counts were compared with the published prize schedules. Enterprises led teams by 28.84 percentage points for any award and by 11.22 points for first through third prizes. Teams led by 1.40 points for first prize. Noncash excellence awards accounted for 17.62 points of the overall enterprise advantage. Capping scheduled places at the number of finalists reproduced all 96 grade counts across 24 brackets. Of 4,479 pairs of finalists who competed in the same bracket, a winner flag distinguished 1,645 and the full grades distinguished 3,043. Separating excellence awards from the three monetary grades recovered 1,155 of the 1,398 distinctions that grades add to the winner flag. For studies of entrepreneurial certification, recording three outcomes at announcement (no award, noncash recognition and a cash-bearing prize) keeps public recognition distinct from eligibility for prize money.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Anyone reading the published results of Shenzhen’s city innovation competition could fairly conclude that registered enterprises outperform entrepreneurial teams. Across the 2024 and 2025 industry finals, 212 of 253 enterprise entries appeared on an award list, compared with 111 of 202 team entries. Yet the two tracks won exactly the same number of first prizes. Both statements are true. They differ only in what the reader takes “winning” to mean.

The point is not pedantic. Research that uses competition outcomes relies on two different mechanisms. One treats a prize as finance: McKenzie’s experiment with business plan grants in Nigeria (McKenzie, 2017) measured what firms did once they obtained capital. The other treats a prize as certification: Howell (2020) found that success in a venture competition raised the likelihood of later financing, even for some winners who received no cash, because the result told outside investors something about the venture. Signalling arguments of this kind depend on two properties of an award: observers must be able to see it, and it must separate some entrants from others (Mochkabadi et al., 2024; Roccapriore et al., 2025). A dataset that collapses every published prize into one winner flag keeps the first property and can destroy the second. It may also attach a cash interpretation to awards that carried none.

Shenzhen’s competition makes both properties measurable. The organizing committee runs parallel industry finals for locally registered enterprises and for entrepreneurial teams, and for each edition it issues three documents: a finalist list, a plan stating how many prizes of each grade each track may award in each industry, and an award list naming the recipients. The first defines who reached the final. The second fixes the number of places before anyone is judged. The third shows who filled them. Read together, they reveal how much of an apparent enterprise advantage was already written into the rules once the finalists were known.

This study uses these records to answer three questions. At which grade does the enterprise–team difference change sign, and how much of it comes from awards without prize money? How closely do the published schedules, capped at the size of each finalist roster, reproduce the observed counts? And how many comparisons between finalists who actually competed against one another are lost when only a winner flag is kept? Supplementary analyses bound the 2023 comparison, for which the industry assignments of 23 team finalists are not available in the study records, and simulate a different division of the same places between the tracks.

The study makes three contributions. First, it shows with complete public records that, together, the published schedules and finalist counts reproduced the number of awards at every grade in all 24 brackets, so the headline gap between the tracks can be accounted for by the allocation of places, without reference to how projects were judged. Second, it quantifies the resolution of each coding scheme by counting the within-bracket pairs of finalists to which the scheme assigns different outcomes. Third, it turns these counts into a coding rule for researchers who link competition results to later financing, namely to keep at least the boundary between noncash recognition and cash-bearing prizes. More broadly, the case separates two decisions that are easily confused: the panel’s decision about rank and the organizer’s decision about how many places to publish and which of them carry money.

The distinction also depends on who reads the result. For an observer who already knows the finalist roster, the winner flag distinguishes ventures within a bracket only when some finalists receive no award. A lender or customer meeting a venture for the first time may value the published name regardless, and even an informed observer can learn from the grade. Where every finalist in a bracket won something, the flag itself separated no one within that bracket. The analysis measures how often this happened, using the smallest units to which the rules applied.

Section 2 sets out what a published award does and does not record. Section 3 describes the records and methods, Section 4 reports the results, and Section 5 discusses the implications for organizers and researchers and the limits of the evidence.

sec.title: 2. What an award records
2.1. The public meaning of a win
sec.p: A competition generates several kinds of evidence. An application records a founder’s decision to enter; a score records an evaluator’s judgement; a published prize records a position in the organizer’s ranking. Later investment and survival are separate outcomes again. Dana et al. (2023) review how competitions connect nascent ventures with audiences and resources, and Dvouletý (2023) follows participants in a Czech contest to examine their survival and performance afterwards. Shenzhen’s notices make it possible to follow an entry from the finalist roster to the award list, but not into the market.

Even inside the final, a prize compresses a good deal. Gius (2024) shows that disagreement among judges carries information about later startup success, so two projects with similar mean scores may have received very different assessments. An award list removes that variation. It also hides an earlier decision: where in each ranking the organizer drew the line. For a study of judging, the missing information is the distribution of individual scores. For a study of how a city distributes recognition, it is the number of eligible finalists and the number of places offered to them.

Taking part can matter apart from the result. Research on pitching traces the process from preparation through presentation to later action (McSweeney et al., 2025), and a field experiment found that pitch training changed entrepreneurs’ subsequent participation in other competitions and support programmes (Clingingsmith et al., 2023). An entrant may therefore gain from the final without ever appearing on an award list. Recognition, by contrast, reaches people who never heard the pitch, which is why studies of external endorsements and investment decisions pay close attention to the audience receiving the signal (Mochkabadi et al., 2024; Roccapriore et al., 2025). The Shenzhen lists capture a single moment in that sequence: the city’s decision to attach a public distinction to an entry.

This matters most when the lower tiers carry no cash. Howell (2020) observed a financing response among ventures near a competition cutoff, including some that won no money. That finding is a reason to keep Shenzhen’s excellence awards when recognition is the outcome, and an equally good reason to code them separately. Without the distinction, a higher winning rate could mean wider publicity, a larger share of finalists eligible for prize money, or a larger share holding the top distinction, and the analyst cannot tell which.

sec.title: 2.2. Where organizational status enters the competition
sec.p: In Shenzhen, local registration status decided which track a project could enter. Enterprise finalists were ventures already registered in the eligible jurisdiction. The team track admitted projects that lacked that registration but intended to establish a local presence (Shenzhen Science & Technology Innovation Bureau, 2024; Shenzhen Science & Technology Innovation Bureau, 2025). A team could therefore include experienced founders or technology developed elsewhere, and describing all team entrants as less mature would read into the rules a distinction they do not make.

The industry bracket mattered as much as the track. An information technology project competed only for the places reserved for its field, and unfilled places in a small vehicle bracket did not pass to other industries. Any citywide comparison therefore mixes three quantities: each track’s industry mix, the number of finalists in each industry, and the depth of the prize list available to each group.

Contest-design research asks how prize structures shape the effort contestants supply, and models of centralized assignment ask who competes for which prizes (Barbieri & Serena, 2024; Liu & Kim, 2023). Testing such responses would require data on potential entrants and the timing of their decisions. Shenzhen’s published rules support a narrower question: once the finalists had qualified, how many awards could the organizer distribute in each track? Holding entrants fixed isolates that administrative choice and makes explicit what a behavioural model would have to relax.

These features supply two checks on any enterprise advantage. If the gap shrinks once both tracks receive the same industry and year weights, composition is responsible. If it survives in a bracket where both tracks had the same number of finalists, the planned award numbers can be compared directly. The information technology finals provide that second comparison in two consecutive years.

sec.title: 2.3. Organizational intermediaries and the allocation of attention
sec.p: An organizer decides which part of a private evaluation becomes public. The finalist notice names the projects admitted to the municipal round; the later notice names the prize recipients and assigns each a grade. Between the two sits a decision seldom visible in venture-level data: how many names from each ranking the city intends to publish.

Accelerator research separates the services a programme provides from the characteristics of the ventures it admits (Assenova & Amit, 2024; Fehder, 2024). Shenzhen makes the corresponding distinction visible at registration. A registered company and an entrepreneurial team can reach the same industry final yet be ranked separately, and the track printed on the finalist notice shows which prize list applied.

For founders, an introduction to an investor, feedback on a pitch and an award are different returns to taking part. Introductions depend on access to investors (Dalle et al., 2025), feedback can arrive before any financing decision (Quignon, 2023), and founders may turn down the terms an investor offers (Sturm et al., 2025). An award list records only one of these exchanges. It shows that the city named a project in public; evidence of an introduction or an investment has to come from elsewhere.

Ecosystem studies examine relationships among institutions (Wurth et al., 2022), links between regional resources and entrepreneurial activity (Queissner et al., 2024), and the resource combinations associated with high-impact entrepreneurship (Tekic & Tekic, 2025). The unit of observation in this study is much smaller: a dated prize list recording one institution’s action towards named projects, which can be checked against another document the same institution issued before the winners were known. Organizers of external innovation contests also gain relationships of their own from contact with entrants (Cavallo & Burgers, 2025), so a long list of recognized firms may serve the city even if it does little to separate the projects in a final. The Shenzhen notices allow both quantities to be measured: how many ventures were named, and how many competitors their grades distinguish.

sec.title: 2.4. Registration, evaluation and the meaning of a grade
sec.p: Research on firm emergence examines the resource commitments and signals that accompany the move to a formal organization (Colombo et al., 2024). Nothing in that work implies that an unregistered project is new to its industry. The Shenzhen criterion concerns local registration at a given date: an experienced founder might enter a team project before incorporating locally, and a registered enterprise might submit a project at an early technical stage. The analysis therefore keeps the original admission categories instead of relabelling them as stages of maturity.

A young firm often has to explain both why its technology is distinctive and why outsiders should take it seriously. Work on cultural entrepreneurship shows how firms build accounts of themselves to secure legitimacy and resources (Lounsbury & Glynn, 2001). An award helps because it has an identifiable issuer and a date, which makes it easier to verify than the firm’s own story. Its meaning still depends on the event. A first prize in a separately ranked team final places a project at the top of that year’s eligible teams; it says much less about where the same project would have stood among registered enterprises. The name of a prize travels further than the rules that gave it meaning.

Resource providers look for different information when they evaluate a startup (Wesley II et al., 2022), and grants, accelerators and equity crowdfunding tell observers different things about how a venture obtained support (Ahmad, 2025). For a researcher compiling venture histories from public announcements, the fact that the city awarded a prize can be coded with confidence. Coding it as independent validation of quality requires information about its selectivity, and coding it as finance requires a monetary entitlement. A single-city setting shows how often these distinctions arise without variation in national funding systems, language or the names of grades.

Judging can vary even among entrants facing the same schedule. Studies of pitch competitions link entrepreneur attributes to investment evaluations (Hoorvitch Lavi & Yaniv, 2023), field experiments examine how investors respond to otherwise comparable approaches from different founders (Gornall & Strebulaev, 2025), and foreign startups pose evaluation problems of their own (Wright et al., 2023). These studies identify the variables a study of panels would want to collect. They also explain why a large gap in award rates should prompt a look at the available places before it is attributed to the panel. In a bracket with a place for every finalist, judges could disagree sharply about the best entrants and every entrant would still be recognized.

Technology adds a further layer. Research on the first financing rounds of technology-based firms examines combinations of signals (Passavanti et al., 2024), and a city has good reason to convene panels with different technical expertise. Yet sector membership also has an administrative consequence. A medical device that competed in the information technology final faced that final’s schedule, whatever industry an analyst might assign after reading its title. For estimating available recognition, the relevant sector is the one in which the city made the award.

sec.title: 2.5. The place of the award schedule in contest design
sec.p: In contest models, prizes affect effort or the decision to enter (Dong et al., 2025; Zhang, 2024). Shenzhen’s finalist notices fix the population at a later point. Once a bracket has 20 named projects, whether it can award 22 distinct places can be checked directly; whether a different announcement would have attracted two more entrants is a question for application records.

A city can reserve one first prize per track and still give finalists very different chances of winning it. With three finalists the prize covers a third of the field; with five, a fifth. The 2024 vehicle final had exactly these roster sizes. Which division an organizer prefers depends on what the prize is for, a question that is also central to models of multi-prize contests (Feng et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025).

The analysis uses the actual brackets to separate three situations that a citywide rate combines. Equal finalist numbers expose differences in the places offered. Equal prize counts expose differences in roster size. Following the same projects down the prize list, from first place to excellence, shows where the track comparison changes sign.

sec.title: 3. Records and methods
3.1. Editions, entrants and award categories
sec.p: The unit of observation was an entry announced for a Shenzhen municipal industry final. An organization listed with two distinct projects contributed two entries. District qualifiers, overseas competitions, national rounds and special challenges were excluded. Aggregate participation figures often cover several of these events, so they cannot serve as denominators for awards made at the municipal industry final.

The competition office released separate enterprise and team finalist notices in 2023 (Organizing Committee Office of the 15th China Shenzhen Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition, 2023a; Organizing Committee Office of the 15th China Shenzhen Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition, 2023b), published both tracks together in 2024 and 2025 (Shenzhen Competition Organizing Committee Office, 2024a; Organizing Committee Office of the 17th China Shenzhen Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition, 2025), and issued an award notice after each final (China Shenzhen Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition Organizing Committee Office, 2023; China Shenzhen Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition Organizing Committee Office, 2024; Shenzhen Competition Organizing Committee Office, 2025). Table 1 distinguishes announced finalist totals from the individual entries available for linkage. Both tracks have complete rosters in 2024 and 2025, giving 455 entries for the main comparison. Award rates used announced finalists as the denominator, so an invited project that did not pitch still counted; attendance and withdrawal records would be needed to compute rates per completed pitch.

caption.title: Coverage of finalist and award records

sec.p: The rules separated first, second and third prizes from excellence awards. Only the former carried a stated monetary prize, subject to the applicable payment conditions; a notice on claiming the 2023 prizes, for example, tied part of a team’s payment to local incorporation (Organizing Committee Office of the China Shenzhen Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition, 2023). The award list identifies the prize announced. It cannot show when, or whether, the recipient collected the money.

The 2023 edition was used as supplementary evidence. Its enterprise roster has 161 entries. The September notice (Organizing Committee Office of the 15th China Shenzhen Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition, 2023b) announced 93 team finalists across seven industries and listed a finalist roster as an attachment. The records available for this analysis identify the industries of the 70 team award recipients. The industry assignments of the other 23 finalists are not available in the records used for this study. The number of awards that year also differs by one between sources. The current text of the official result notice reports 205 recipients (China Shenzhen Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition Organizing Committee Office, 2023), whereas the archived workbook contains 206 numbered rows with 206 distinct entrant names and project titles, the figure also given in contemporary press coverage (Wang, 2023). The roster count was used to describe the extraction, and 2023 was kept outside the primary comparison. The available evidence does not identify which entry, if any, accounts for the discrepancy.

sec.title: 3.2. Linking projects and aligning industries
sec.p: Finalist and award lists normally identify both the entrant and the project, but either field alone can be ambiguous: one organization may submit several projects, and a project title may survive a change in how a team’s name is written. Source row identifiers were kept throughout extraction. Text broken across lines in the PDFs (Portable Document Format files) was rejoined, and spacing, punctuation, case and full-width characters were normalized before names were compared.

Matching was carried out within edition and track, with exact agreement on both fields taking priority. For the remaining candidates, a character-sequence similarity score was computed separately for entrant and title (twice the length of matched character blocks divided by the combined string length). A link was accepted automatically if one field matched exactly and the other scored at least 0.50, or if both scored at least 0.85. Candidates were ranked by mean score, with a bonus of 0.20 when one field matched exactly and the other scored at least 0.45, and automatic acceptance required a lead of at least 0.08 over the next candidate. Ambiguous cases were reviewed against the published text. Each finalist could be linked to at most one award, and the final counts were compared with totals taken directly from the award lists. That last check catches entries misplaced across industries or grades, though not an exchange of identities within the same category.

Across the recoverable rosters, 424 award entries matched exactly on both fields, 33 satisfied the corroboration rule and two required manual review. Both reviewed entries were 2024 team excellence awards: one involved a discrepancy in the entrant name attached to a distinctive satellite-imaging project, the other a difference between traditional and simplified characters. All results for the complete years were also recomputed without these two links.

Two industry classifications were needed. For the schedule check, the analysis retained the seven industries in which the 2024 awards were actually made and the five used in 2025. For comparisons across years, new energy, new-energy vehicles and environmental technology were combined in both years to match the 2025 green and low-carbon bracket; the other four domains kept their competition labels. Merging industries before applying a year’s schedule could move unfilled places between finals that were in fact held separately, so the cap was always applied in the original brackets before any aggregation. Keeping both versions of industry membership allows the historical material to be used without imposing a later edition’s rules on projects that entered an earlier one.

The linkage problem also depends on the level at which a result is reported. A citywide count at a given grade can be read from one award list, but a claim that a particular finalist reached that grade requires a match across lists. Classical record linkage separates agreement from the evidential weight of agreement (Fellegi & Sunter, 1969); recent reviews stress the choices involved in defining comparisons and handling uncertain links (Thibaudeau, 2025), and prediction-based methods show how several fields can improve discrimination among candidates (Moretti & Shlomo, 2023). Here, an exact match on a long, distinctive project title is worth far more than a shared short expression in two names, and the corroborating entrant field and the required lead over the next candidate guard against accepting a generic project description as identification.

Checks were made at three levels. Each accepted link must be unique within the finalist file for its track and edition. The matched grades must sum to the counts independently available from the award notice. And changing a judgement-dependent link should affect only the results to which that entry contributes: dropping a team excellence link lowers the team award rate but must leave every enterprise numerator and the team podium count unchanged. Passing one level is not enough. A group total can be correct even if two projects with the same grade swap identities, and a plausible individual match cannot repair an incomplete finalist denominator.

sec.title: 3.3. Comparisons on a common finalist denominator
sec.p: Each finalist contributed one observation to the denominator at each threshold, and an award recipient was counted at the threshold reached and at every broader one. The enterprise–team difference was calculated as the enterprise rate minus the team rate, in percentage points. To show how each grade contributes, the cumulative totals were also split into three mutually exclusive categories (excellence only, second or third prize, and first prize), whose rate differences sum to the overall difference. All percentages and differences were computed before rounding.

The pooled comparison weights every finalist equally within a track, so it can reflect differences in the industries and years in which each track had more entrants. Kitagawa’s symmetric decomposition (Kitagawa, 1955) was used to separate these contributions. For each domain-year, the difference between the two tracks’ award rates was multiplied by the mean of their finalist shares in that cell; summing these products gave the within-cell component. The difference in shares multiplied by the mean award rate, summed across cells, gave the composition component. The gap was also recomputed with equal weights for the ten domain-years and with weights proportional to total finalists in each.

The announced rosters cover the full population for the two main editions. Applying the published schedules to these rosters reproduced all 96 observed grade counts (Section 4.3). The realized differences for 2024 and 2025 are reported, and their sensitivity to the two manually reviewed links and to the choice of weights is examined. Section 4.4 treats 2023 separately and bounds the comparisons that depend on the unknown industry assignments of 23 team finalists.

sec.title: 3.4. Reconstructing the prize lists
sec.p: For each original industry, track and year, the planned cumulative number of places at a given threshold was capped at the number of announced finalists: H = min(Q, N), where Q is the number of places in the schedule and N the finalist count. The observed count B came from the award notice, and B−H measured any departure from the schedule. With 12 industry-years, two tracks and three cumulative thresholds, the comparison covered 72 counts. Agreement at all three thresholds pinned down the numbers of first prizes, combined second and third prizes, and excellence awards. The four individual grades were also checked: starting from first prize, each grade received the smaller of its planned places and the remaining finalists, and the rest passed to the next grade. This gave a separate benchmark for each of 96 industry-year, track and grade combinations.

The 2024 plan allowed adjustments where entry was low, so the published schedules were applied to the seven industries in which finals were actually held. The benchmark is thus conditional on the implemented bracket structure and the published rosters. It can be computed without knowing who won, and it makes no claim about how many entrants would reach each final when the competition first opened.

sec.title: 3.5. Incomplete denominators and an alternative award schedule
sec.p: In 2023, each of the 23 team finalists without a listed award could belong to any of the five harmonized domains. For a given allocation, the team denominator in a domain equalled its known winners plus the unawarded projects assigned to it. All 17,550 nonnegative integer allocations summing to 23 were enumerated, and for each the enterprise–team gap was computed with equal domain weights and with weights based on enterprise finalist counts. The minimum and maximum gave jointly attainable bounds conditional on the extracted team award roster (Horowitz &amp; Manski, 2006). Assigning all 23 finalists to each domain in turn gave marginal bounds for that domain, but those extremes cannot occur together.

For the two complete years, a separate exercise asked what a different division of the available prizes would mean for exactly the same finalists. Within each original industry-year, the combined numbers of first prizes, first-to-third prizes and all awards were held at their observed values. Integer allocations to enterprises were enumerated, and the remainder at each threshold was given to teams, subject to first prizes not exceeding podium places, podium places not exceeding all awards, and awards not exceeding finalists in either track. Among feasible allocations, the one selected minimized the sum of squared track-rate differences across the three thresholds, weighted equally. Ties were broken in favour of the smallest total absolute change to the observed enterprise counts, then by a fixed ordering of solutions.

Two summaries are reported. The pooled difference describes both editions together. The mean absolute difference gives each of the 12 industry-years equal weight and stops differences of opposite sign from cancelling. The exercise fixed the number of places at the three thresholds; it imposed no monetary budget and did not preserve the separate second- and third-prize totals within each track.

sec.title: 3.6. Measuring when an award distinguishes finalists
sec.p: Pair counts used the 455 individually listed finalists from 2024 and 2025 (253 enterprise and 202 team entries); 2023 contributed no pairs. Two entries formed an eligible pair if they competed in the same year, original industry bracket and track. A bracket with N finalists and B awardees contains B(N−B) pairs made up of one awardee and one finalist without an award, out of N(N−1)/2 unordered pairs in total. The ratio is the share of pairs that a binary award record distinguishes.

Each finalist was then classified by the published result: no award, excellence, third, second or first prize. Subtracting same-category pairs from the total in each bracket gave the number distinguished by grade. Every winner–nonwinner pair separated by the binary code remains separated, so the additional pairs consist entirely of winners who received different grades. A first–second pair adds one distinction, as does a first–excellence pair; the count uses only the published labels and makes no assumption about the distance between grades.

All 24 brackets in the two complete editions contain at least two finalists. Counting each unordered pair once within its bracket and summing gave every eligible pair equal weight. As an alternative, the share within each bracket was computed and averaged across the 24 brackets. The first quantity describes a pair drawn from the full list of eligible comparisons; the second describes a final chosen with equal probability, followed by a pair drawn within it.

The count can be reproduced directly from the finalist file by listing every pair of distinct entries within the same original final and cross-tabulating their outcomes. The upper triangle of the resulting five-by-five table contains pairs with different outcomes, and the diagonal contains ties. Summing the cells that join no award to any winning grade gives the binary count; summing all cells above the diagonal gives the graded count. The two routes, from bracket totals and from direct enumeration, must give identical totals. A disagreement would point to a bracket assignment, a duplicate entry or the treatment of an unawarded finalist.

The rules (Shenzhen Science and Technology Innovation Bureau, 2024; Shenzhen Science and Technology Innovation Bureau, 2025) attached monetary prizes to first, second and third place and none to excellence awards. A three-category record of no award, excellence and podium therefore preserves the distinction relevant to prize eligibility. Splitting winners into excellence and podium recipients recovers the pairs that cross this boundary; keeping all three podium grades then recovers pairs of cash-prize winners at different grades. Whether a particular podium winner met the payment conditions and received the money is a matter for disbursement records.

To check the influence of the two manually reviewed team excellence links, both projects were kept on their finalist rosters and the pair counts were recomputed with the two award links removed. Keeping the finalists holds the pair denominator fixed and isolates the linkage decision. Section 4.7 reports the linkage check and compares pair-weighted and bracket-weighted percentages.

sec.title: 4. Results
4.1. The prize grades behind the enterprise advantage
sec.p: In the two editions with complete rosters, enterprise entrants received 212 awards from 253 finalist places and teams 111 from 202. Counting every listed award, the enterprise rate exceeded the team rate by 28.84 percentage points. Restricting the outcome to prizes with a stated monetary award cut the difference to 11.22 points. At first prize the order reversed: fourteen enterprises and fourteen teams won first prizes, or 5.53% of enterprise finalists and 6.93% of team finalists. Table 2 gives the counts, and Figure 1 compares the two tracks at each threshold.

caption.title: Note: Award counts and rates among finalists, 2024–2025
Recognition at three award thresholds, 2024–2025

sec.p: Splitting the awards into mutually exclusive grades shows where the reversal comes from. Excellence awards went to 131 enterprise entries and 69 team entries. Relative to the two finalist pools, they contributed 17.62 points, or 61.1% of the net enterprise advantage. Second and third prizes together added 12.62 points, and first prizes subtracted 1.40. More than half of the overall advantage thus arose at the one tier that carried no cash. Removing excellence awards still leaves a sizeable gap; removing second and third prizes as well changes which track comes out ahead.

The same pattern holds within each complete edition. In 2024, 128 of 153 enterprises and 68 of 117 teams received an award; in 2025 the figures were 84 of 100 and 43 of 85. Enterprise recognition stayed close to 84% even though the number of enterprise winners fell by 44. The team rate moved more, from 58.12% to 50.59%, as the team finalist pool shrank by 32 entries and its winners by 25. First prizes were split evenly in both years, eight per track in 2024 and six per track in 2025, so the pooled result is not an artefact of combining an enterprise-favouring year with a team-favouring one.

The choice of denominator can also reverse an impression in a less visible way. Among podium winners, 14 of 81 enterprises and 14 of 42 teams held a first prize. Those fractions describe the composition of each track’s podium. A founder who has just qualified for the final faces a different reference group: all 253 enterprise finalists or all 202 team finalists. The difference matters whenever a table of winners is used to infer the opportunities available at an earlier stage.

The intermediate threshold locates the reversal precisely. Enterprises won 42 first or second prizes and teams 28, or 16.60% and 13.86% of their finalists. The enterprise advantage of 2.74 points is therefore present before third prizes are counted; adding them raises it to 11.22 points, and excellence awards produce the largest further increase. A reader does not need the two extreme definitions of an award to see the reversal, because the line between first prize and the next grade is enough. Figure 2 shows the contribution of each mutually exclusive grade; the contributions can be added because every finalist appears in at most one grade.

caption.title: Contribution of each prize grade to the overall track difference

sec.p: Table 3 gives the annual counts, including 2023, for which the overall team denominator is known. In 2023, 48 of 161 enterprise finalists and 24 of 93 team finalists won at least a third prize, and each track received eight first prizes. In 2024 the team podium and first-prize counts stayed at 24 and eight while team finalists rose from 93 to 117, so selectivity increased with no change in the prizes on offer. The 2025 edition moved the other way on roster size: team finalists fell to 85, but the podium total fell to 18 and first prizes to six. Broad recognition, the monetary threshold and first prize thus moved by different amounts within the same track. Figure 3 plots the annual rates on a common scale.

caption.title: Finalists and award thresholds by edition and track
Annual award rates on a common finalist denominator

sec.title: 4.2. Finalists in the same industry and year
sec.p: An enterprise advantage at the broadest threshold appears in all ten harmonized industry-years, ranging from 7.60 points in the combined green and low-carbon domain in 2024 to 48.00 points in information technology in the same year. The citywide gap is almost entirely a difference within industries and years, not a difference in where the two tracks entered: of the pooled 28.84 points, 28.81 come from the within-cell component and 0.03 from composition (Table 4).

caption.title: Industry composition and alternative weights, 2024–2025

sec.p: The information technology finals offer a comparison that needs no weighting. In 2024 each track admitted 25 projects. The enterprise plan offered 12 podium places and 14 excellence awards, enough to recognize all 25 finalists; the team plan offered six podium places and seven excellence awards. The results listed 25 enterprise winners and 13 team winners, and each track received two first prizes. A 48-point overall gap and a zero first-prize gap thus arose in the same industry, in the same year, with identical roster sizes. Nothing about the relative maturity of enterprise and team projects is needed to explain those counts.

The same industry again admitted equal numbers in 2025, 20 projects per track, and its overall gap was 45.00 points. The result is not confined to these two brackets. Excluding information technology leaves a pooled enterprise advantage of 24.87 points for any award; excluding the combined green and low-carbon domain instead raises it to 33.68 points. The podium and first-prize comparisons keep their direction under both exclusions.

The green and low-carbon results also show the cost of harmonizing across years. In 2024 the label combines three industry finals, one of which admitted only three enterprise finalists in new-energy vehicles. In 2025 the organizers used a single bracket, in which 16 of 20 enterprises and eight of 16 teams won an award, a 30-point gap. The common label allows a broad comparison, but only the original categories identify projects that competed for the same places.

In the four industries whose labels did not change, Table 5 shows considerable variation behind the two-year averages. In 2024 biomedicine and advanced equipment each admitted 25 enterprises and 19 teams and made 20 enterprise and ten team awards, so their track gaps were identical. In 2025 both again admitted 20 enterprises and recognized 16 enterprise and eight team finalists, but biomedicine admitted 16 teams and equipment 18. The gap rose to 30.00 points in biomedicine and to 35.56 points in equipment, a difference that lies entirely in the team denominators. Identical award counts in similar industries can thus conceal different per-finalist rates.

caption.title: Award coverage in the original industry finals

sec.p: New materials add a complementary case. In 2024 its enterprise schedule produced the same 20 winners from 25 finalists as biomedicine and equipment, while its team roster had 20 finalists and ten awards. The same ten team awards therefore covered exactly half the team finalists in new materials and slightly more than half in the other two industries. In 2025 new materials had only 15 team finalists, against 16 in biomedicine and 18 in equipment, and its eight team awards reached a majority. A city report giving eight team awards in each industry would be accurate, yet it would leave out what a finalist needs to judge how widely the competition’s recognition extended.

The 2024 vehicle final lies at the other end of the size distribution. Only three enterprise and five team projects reached it, and all eight received an award. One first prize per track translated into rates of one third and one fifth, so at the top threshold enterprises led in this industry, the reverse of the pooled ordering. Combining the vehicle final with energy and environmental technology makes the harmonized domain comparable with the later green bracket, but it also hides this configuration. Figure 4 therefore uses the native categories.

caption.title: Coverage of any award in the original industry brackets

sec.p: Composition deserves a second look even though its aggregate contribution is close to zero. In a symmetric decomposition each cell has its own signed contribution, and cells can offset one another. For any award, the 2024 green and low-carbon domain contributed about +3.18 points to the composition component and information technology in the same year about −1.90 points, each far larger than the net +0.03. The small total means that equalizing the observed mix barely changes the pooled answer. It does not mean that the two tracks had the same industry distribution, or that composition was negligible in every industry. Figure 5 shows the signed contributions.

caption.title: Signed composition contributions to the any-award gap

sec.title: 4.3. How closely the rules reproduce the results
sec.p: Table 6 compares planned, roster-capped and published counts. The 2024 plans implied 219 places across all tiers if each of the seven industries filled its schedule, but the actual finalist numbers could support only 196. Most of the shortfall arose in new-energy vehicles, where the cap removed 17 nominal enterprise places and five team places; the remainder was one enterprise place in information technology. The cap also removed three podium places, all in the enterprise vehicle bracket. These local shortages would disappear from view if the two track totals were capped only after pooling industries.

caption.title: Planned, attainable and observed award places

sec.p: The 2025 plan offered 129 places. Its enterprise information technology bracket offered 22 awards to 20 finalists, reducing the attainable total by two, while all 54 podium places remained available. Over the two years there were 348 nominal and 323 attainable awards, including 123 of 126 nominal podium places, and every one of the 28 planned first prizes could be filled. The award notices reported exactly the attainable totals at all three thresholds, and the checks of first, second, third and excellence awards matched in all 96 cases. Enterprises received 28 second and 39 third prizes; teams received 14 at each grade. These contributed 4.14 and 8.48 points to the overall gap, which is why an account focused only on first prizes and excellence awards would still miss part of the difference.

Agreement also held in each of the 72 industry-year, track and cumulative-threshold comparisons, so the residual in the pooled gap is zero at every threshold. This matters most in small brackets, where agreement only at city level could hide an extra award in one industry offset by an unfilled place in another. A perfect match still leaves one question open. Any ordering of competitors that filled the same places would have produced these counts, and the archive names the recipients without giving the scores needed to compare one ordering with another.

The difference between nominal and attainable places is sharpest at the bottom of the grade ladder. With three companies in the 2024 vehicle final, one first prize and two second prizes exhausted the enterprise roster, giving published tier counts of one, two, zero and zero. The team track in the same industry filled a first, second and third prize and recognized its two remaining finalists at excellence. Full recognition can thus make the overall win indicator uninformative while the distribution of grades still differs between the tracks.

Elsewhere the cap bound at a different point. Enterprise information technology could fill all its planned podium places in both years; the roster ran out further down, where the last excellence awards would have needed more entrants. For anyone budgeting recognition the difference is real: in one case nominal monetary places went unfilled, in the other the shortage fell entirely on noncash recognition. Subtracting unfilled places from the citywide total recovers the right number of omitted awards but loses this distinction. Figure 6 identifies the brackets responsible for the shortfall.

caption.title: Nominal places lost to the finalist cap, by grade

sec.p: The small vehicle final also allows a check on how far the conclusions depend on a sector with special low-entry provisions. Excluding it in 2024 leaves 250 enterprise and 197 team finalists across the two editions. The broad comparison then becomes 209 awards against 106, a gap of 29.79 points; the podium gap is 11.40 points and the first-prize gap −1.40. Unlike dropping the whole harmonized green and low-carbon domain, this removes only eight projects in the one year in which the vehicle final was unusually small. The citywide ordering survives either treatment, while any interpretation of the small industry itself depends on keeping its native structure, as recorded in the final notice (Shenzhen Competition Organizing Committee Office, 2024b).

sec.title: 4.4. Bounds for the 2023 edition
sec.p: The 2023 team finalist notice fixes the overall denominator. Using the 70 extracted team winners as both numerator and denominator would give a meaningless recognition rate of 100%; using the 93 announced finalists gives 75.27%. Sector rates need more care. Thirteen information technology teams won an award, so the number of team finalists in that domain could lie anywhere between 13 and 36. The 27 winning green and low-carbon teams imply a range of 27 to 50, and each of the other three domains, with ten winning teams, has a marginal denominator between ten and 33.

Across every feasible allocation of the missing industry labels, teams had the higher first-prize rate. With equal domain weights the enterprise-minus-team gap ranged from −5.29 to −3.14 points, and with enterprise-roster weights from −5.21 to −3.50. By contrast, the equal-weight intervals for any award (−6.08 to 12.78) and for podium prizes (−0.93 to 5.52) both cross zero, as do the enterprise-weighted intervals (−5.61 to 9.35 and −0.71 to 4.42). The 2023 edition therefore supports the direction of the first-prize comparison, conditional on the extracted winners, but cannot sign the industry-standardized broad award gap. This uncertainty concerns the location of the 23 unawarded teams and is separate from the one-entry discrepancy between the 2023 notice and roster.

The two reviewed team links in the complete years give a different kind of check. Dropping both lowers the team recognition numerator from 111 to 109 with the 202 finalists unchanged, which raises the pooled any-award gap from 28.84 to 29.83 points. Because both were excellence awards, neither the podium nor the first-prize comparison changes.

The bounds should be read with the nature of the missing information in mind. All 70 listed team awardees have a known industry and grade; the uncertainty concerns only finalists without an award. Adding such an entrant to a sector raises its denominator without changing any numerator, which can shift a small sector’s first-prize rate considerably and a large sector’s much less. Dividing the missing entries in proportion to known winners would look precise, but it would assume a relation between industry and award receipt for which the notices give no evidence.

Each endpoint describes an allocation consistent with all the records, including the requirement that sector totals sum to 93. Table 7 gives the jointly attainable ranges. Under equal weights the broad gap could be slightly negative or clearly positive, while the first-prize interval stays negative even at its upper end. A directional conclusion is thus available at the most selective threshold without imputing the missing labels. That is more informative than discarding the edition, and it keeps a negative first-prize result distinct from an unsigned overall comparison.

caption.title: Joint bounds for the 2023 standardized track difference
Jointly attainable industry-standardized differences in 2023

sec.p: Figure 7 also shows that a narrower interval need not reflect better record coverage. The same 23 missing labels enter every threshold, but first prizes have small numerators, so reallocating unawarded finalists moves the first-prize rate less on the percentage-point scale. Recovering the authentic sector roster for those team entrants would turn a set of feasible values into an observed comparison without changing the known overall team count. Locating the uncertainty precisely helps set priorities for any future recovery of records.

sec.title: 4.5. A different division of the existing places
sec.p: How many places would have to change tracks for award rates within each industry to be similar? In the fixed-total exercise, enterprises receive 180 of the 323 available awards and teams 143, a net transfer of 32 awards to the team track. Fourteen of the 32 are podium places, so adding the two figures would double-count. The first-prize allocation is unchanged in every industry-year. Table 8 reports the resulting rates as differences between tracks.

caption.title: Fixed-total reallocation within the 12 original industry-years

sec.p: Table 8 and Figure 8 show how the local changes add up. The pooled any-award difference falls to 0.35 points, but the local comparison says more about how close the schedule comes to its objective. With equal weight for each industry-year, the mean absolute difference falls from 26.82 to 2.40 points for any award and from 14.32 to 2.20 points for podium prizes. Some local difference remains even where pooled rates are close, because a single indivisible place can move a rate substantially in a small final. The first-prize mean absolute difference stays at 2.28 points.

caption.title: Local differences under the published and reallocated schedules

sec.p: The pooled podium gap becomes slightly negative. That is consistent with a criterion defined within industries: the selected schedule nearly equalizes local rates, while the headline rate still weights industries by each track’s finalist numbers. Giving four times the weight to any one threshold in turn produced the same pooled counts and mean absolute gaps. These results quantify the effect of the chosen division of places on the published rosters; they do not predict how future entrants would respond to a different schedule.
Enterprises led by 2.74 percentage points when first and second prizes were combined, whereas teams led by 1.40 points for first prize alone.

sec.title: 4.6. How many comparisons the award grade preserves
sec.p: The 24 original brackets holding the 455 finalists from 2024 and 2025 contain 4,479 distinct within-bracket pairs. Of these, 1,645 consist of one award winner and one entrant without an award, so a reader with only a binary award code could tell apart the members of 36.73% of comparable pairs. The five published outcome categories distinguish 3,043 pairs, or 67.94%, adding 1,398 comparisons in which both finalists won an award but at different grades. All of these distinctions are already present in the public list. Recovering them requires no judges’ scores and no assumption about the value of one grade relative to another. Table 9 breaks these comparisons down by track. Supplementary Table S1 reports the numbers of finalists at each award grade and without an award in each of the 24 brackets.

caption.title: Within-bracket pairs distinguished by published outcomes

sec.p: The loss is considerably larger in the enterprise track. There, a binary outcome distinguishes 756 of 2,753 comparable pairs and the graded outcome 1,857, recovering 1,101 pairs of awardees at different grades. In the team track the binary code distinguishes 889 of 1,726 pairs, and grades add 297. The difference reflects the size of the winning groups as well as the mix of grades: where most enterprises won, counting them all as winners created many ties, whereas team brackets had a more even mix of winners and unawarded finalists. Reporting the 1,101 and 297 alone would hide the fact that the enterprise track also supplied more possible comparisons.

The four fully recognized brackets show the point most clearly. Their 53 entrants form 503 within-bracket pairs, and the binary code ties every one of them, yet the published grades still distinguish 351. The remaining 152 pairs share a grade and cannot be separated at this resolution. Treating such a tie as evidence that judges rated two projects equally would go beyond the records, since a tier groups adjacent parts of a ranking and may contain entrants with quite different scores.

The comparison holds in both years. In 2024 the graded record distinguishes 1,886 of 2,841 pairs, against 1,026 under a binary code; in 2025 the figures are 1,157 of 1,638 and 619. The larger number of pairs in 2024 partly reflects larger brackets, because each added entrant creates a possible pair with every existing member, so pair totals should be read alongside finalist numbers. Figure 9 shows the track-specific percentages for the two codings.

caption.title: Resolution of binary and graded award records within tracks

sec.p: One qualification applies. An analyst linking awards to later financing might want to compare any two firms that later approached the same investor, even if they had competed in different sectors or tracks. Such a study could draw on many more comparisons than those counted here, but at a price: the firms faced different comparison sets and sometimes different numbers of places. The figures reported here identify the comparisons available without crossing those administrative boundaries. They also indicate how heavily a pooled regression on award status would have to rely on differences between brackets if within-bracket support were weak.

sec.title: 4.7. Distinctions lost when grades are dropped
sec.p: Suppose the competition office could release only one field in addition to the winner flag. Of the 1,398 pairs recovered by keeping every grade, 1,155 join an excellence recipient to a podium recipient. A file coding no award, excellence and podium would thus separate 2,800 of the 4,479 pairs, or 62.51%, and keeping first, second and third as separate grades would add the remaining 243. The first step is worth nearly five times the second. For an archive built from brief announcements, the boundary between excellence and the monetary grades is the one to preserve.

Figure 10 shows the underlying counts. The largest group of recovered comparisons pairs an excellence recipient with a third-prize recipient (537 pairs), followed by excellence and second prize (385) and excellence and first prize (233). Among podium recipients, 120 pairs cross the second–third boundary, 69 the first–third boundary and 54 the first–second boundary. Every count refers to projects in the same bracket; two first-prize winners from different industries never enter the tally.

caption.title: Within-bracket pairs with different published outcomes, 2024–2025

sec.p: The first row of Figure 10 shows what the binary code does keep: 1,063 pairs joining an unawarded entrant to an excellence recipient, 235 to a third-prize recipient, 194 to a second-prize recipient and 153 to a first-prize recipient, 1,645 in all. Dropping excellence recipients from a file would be a different and more damaging operation, removing the largest group in this row as well as the 1,155 excellence–podium comparisons. Where the question concerns public exposure, a noncash result separates projects on both sides of the comparison.

The 2024 information technology final allows the calculation to be followed by hand. In the enterprise track the result comprised two first prizes, four second prizes, six third prizes and thirteen excellence awards. Twenty-five entrants form 300 pairs, of which same-grade ties number one among first-prize recipients, six among second-prize recipients, fifteen among third-prize recipients and 78 among excellence recipients. These 100 ties leave 200 distinguishable pairs, every one of which a binary record discards because all 25 projects won something.

The team track in the same final also had 25 finalists and 300 pairs. Twelve went unawarded, seven received excellence awards and two each received first, second and third prizes. Binary coding distinguishes 156 pairs, since each of the 13 awardees can be paired with 12 unawarded finalists, and graded coding distinguishes 210. A binary database would show many comparisons in the team track and none in the enterprise track; with grades, the two are almost level at 210 and 200. Both describe the same judges’ published decisions. What differs is how much of those decisions survives the removal of the prize labels.

Table 10 checks whether these conclusions depend on the largest industry or on the fully recognized brackets. Excluding both information technology finals in both tracks leaves 3,499 pairs, of which 1,390 are distinguished by the binary code and 2,352 by grade. Excluding instead the four brackets in which everyone won leaves 3,976 pairs: all 1,645 binary distinctions survive, because those brackets produced none, and grades distinguish another 1,047. Full recognition makes the problem conspicuous, but it accounts for only 351 of the 1,398 lost distinctions. Most arise in finals where winners and unawarded projects could already be compared.

caption.title: Sensitivity of the within-bracket pair comparison

sec.p: The last row of Table 10 exposes an odd property of binary coding. Treating the two reviewed team excellence links as unmatched raises the number of binary distinctions from 1,645 to 1,650, even though the file has lost two correct award identities. In the equipment team bracket the change moves the split from ten winners and nine unawarded finalists to nine and ten, leaving the product at 90; in environmental technology it moves the split from ten and four to nine and five, raising the product from 40 to 45. The five extra comparisons come purely from a more balanced split and say nothing against the two verified links. Under the graded outcome the same change lowers the count by one, from 3,043 to 3,042.

Bracket-level averaging checks the influence of roster size. With equal weights for the 24 brackets, binary and graded coding distinguish 36.14% and 69.21% of pairs in the typical bracket, against pair-weighted shares of 36.73% and 67.94%. Equal weighting gives the three possible enterprise vehicle pairs in 2024 the same influence as the 300 enterprise information technology pairs in that year. The two weightings differ sharply in a few small fields, but both imply a large loss of resolution. A study whose sampling unit is the final can use the first figure; one drawing comparable pairs from the whole archive can use the second.

Binary status ties 2,834 pairs, and grades break 1,398 of those ties (49.33%). The remaining 1,436 pairs, consisting either of two unawarded finalists or of two ventures with the same prize, mark the limit of the public ranking. Finer comparisons would require scores or more detailed rankings; linking more variables to the award file cannot reveal how the panel ordered two entrants recorded at the same grade.

A researcher interested in access to financial support might instead code every podium recipient as one and everyone else as zero. Under that definition 1,737 within-bracket pairs differ, compared with 1,645 under any-award status. The net increase of 92 hides a much larger change in which projects are compared: only 582 pairs, each joining an unawarded entrant to a podium recipient, are separated under both definitions.

Figure 10 supplies the arithmetic. The 1,063 pairs of an unawarded entrant and an excellence recipient switch from different to tied when the outcome is restricted to cash-bearing grades, while the 1,155 excellence–podium pairs switch from tied to different. The net change is 92, but 2,218 pairs change status. Comparing only the two headline totals would suggest that the outcome definition matters little. In fact, an analyst who chooses the financial definition gains one set of comparisons and gives up another that could be central to a study of public endorsement.

The switch also shifts evidence between the tracks. In the enterprise finals, 510 pairs join an unawarded finalist to an excellence recipient and 912 join an excellence recipient to a podium winner, so moving to the monetary cutoff adds 402 enterprise pairs on net. In the team finals the corresponding counts are 553 and 243, a net loss of 310. A pooled count that barely moves can therefore conceal a marked shift towards observations from the registered-firm competition, which matters for any study estimating a common association between awards and later outcomes across both groups.

Both contrasts can be kept without collecting anything new from entrants. A public-recognition field for all named winners and a cash-bearing field for podium winners together identify the three observed categories, and entering the original grade as well allows second and third prizes to be treated separately where a research question requires it. Disbursement is a separate matter. A blank payment record means something different for an excellence recipient than for a podium recipient whose entitlement depended on local registration, and keeping the grade attached to the payment record allows the two cases to be told apart even in a file compiled long after the awards were made.

sec.title: 5. Discussion
5.1. Reading an award list as evidence about ventures
sec.p: To an observer interested in public recognition, Shenzhen’s enterprise finalists held a clear advantage. To one interested in who reached the top rank, the same lists favour teams by a small margin. The gap between these readings has economic substance. Excellence accounted for 200 of the 323 awards in the complete years. A study defining financial support as appearance on the winners’ list would classify all 200 as cash-prize recipients, while a study of visibility that dropped them would discard almost two-thirds of the names the competition chose to publish.

Four of the 24 original industry-year and track groups awarded a prize to every finalist: the enterprise information technology finals in both years and both new-energy vehicle tracks in 2024. They held 53 of the 455 entrants (11.65%), and full recognition was far more common among enterprises, with 48 of 253 enterprise finalists in these groups against five of 202 team finalists. In the enterprise information technology brackets an indicator for winning any award does not vary at all, so a within-final comparison of recognized and unrecognized enterprises is impossible however detailed the later financing data may be. Podium and first-prize status do vary there. Pooling the two tracks restores variation in broad award status, but part of that variation then comes from the entry rules and prize schedules, and a model using it needs a substantive reason to treat the two groups as comparable.

For a study of the certification channel identified by Howell (2020), the natural Shenzhen comparison starts with excellence recipients and unawarded finalists in the same bracket, which account for 1,063 of the 1,645 pairs separated by the binary indicator. Of the 1,398 distinctions recovered by keeping grades, 1,155 lie between an excellence recipient and a podium winner, both publicly named but only one eligible for prize money. Financing studies should therefore code at least three categories at announcement: no award, noncash excellence and cash-bearing podium. That coding identifies the relevant comparisons. Estimating a financing effect would further require later financing records and a strategy for dealing with selection into grades.

The first-prize result needs the same care. Teams took first prize at a higher rate because the two tracks received the same number of top places for groups of different size. That says little about the relative quality of the two entrant pools. A credible comparison of quality would need to know what judges saw, how panels scored and whether the scoring scale meant the same thing across tracks, which is the kind of evidence Gius (2024) exploits with separate assessments from several judges. Public prize lists answer a narrower question with unusual precision: how far down each ranking the competition extended public recognition.

Two percentages describe different parts of the result and should not be confused. Excellence awards made up 61.9% of all awards, the relevant figure for interpreting a randomly chosen winner’s entry on the list. They also made up 61.1% of the enterprise advantage in award rates, a figure that can be computed only with the finalist lists. Neither measures the share of financial value or the proportion of winners later approached by investors.

sec.title: 5.2. Implications for competition organizers
sec.p: Equal numbers of first prizes and equal first-prize rates are two reasonable but different objectives: the first gives both tracks the same representation among top winners, the second recognizes similar fractions of their finalists. Shenzhen’s schedules met the first and gave the registered-enterprise track many more places in the lower tiers. The documents establish this distribution. Explaining why the city chose it would require evidence from those who designed the competition.

None of this presumes that equal rates are always desirable. In the 2024 information technology final every enterprise was recognized and only about half the teams. An organizer could keep that arrangement, state the intended difference in coverage, and still reserve the same number of first prizes for each track. If similar rates were the aim instead, the two-year exercise shows where the changes would fall: all 28 first prizes could stay where they were, while 32 lower-tier places moved on net. Because 14 of those places carried prize money, an implementation budget would also need the applicable amounts and payment conditions.

Either choice would be easier for entrants to understand if results were published in a compact table giving, for each industry and track, the finalist count, the planned places at each grade and the actual recipients. Readers could then see why a nominal total went unfilled, and where industries were merged for judging, the original entry labels and their mapping to the final bracket could be kept. This matters for year-on-year reporting: in Shenzhen the green and low-carbon grouping had a different administrative meaning in 2025, although many of the underlying projects belonged to the same technological fields as before.

Planning should also be local to each industry. In the 2024 vehicle final, moving one place changes the track gap by more than 53 percentage points because the denominators were three and five. The observed podium gap was +40 points with three podium places per track. Moving one enterprise place to teams gives two of three enterprises and four of five teams, a gap of −13.33 points, and a second transfer would widen the difference again. At the overall threshold there is no margin at all, since eight prizes already went to eight projects. Exact equality at one threshold can coexist with unavoidable inequality at another, so a target such as “equal access” gives administrators no clear direction unless the threshold is specified.

In the 2025 information technology final the difficulty was an odd number of awards: 20 finalists per track and 31 places, so an equal split was impossible. The selected scenario gives enterprises 16 and teams 15, a five-point enterprise advantage; reversing the allocation would give teams the same advantage. The tie-breaking rule favours the smaller departure from the published allocation. Rotating the extra place between tracks across editions could address long-run representation, but evaluating such a policy would require deciding which cohorts count as comparable.

Organizers also have to decide what to weight equally. Giving each industry one vote protects a small final from disappearing into a citywide mean, but it gives an eight-project vehicle final the same standing as a 50-project technology final, whereas weighting entrants equally favours the latter. A programme reporting only a pooled gap close to zero may describe a real improvement for the typical finalist while saying little about a team in a very small bracket. The two summaries in the scenario table answer two different administrative questions: how recognition is distributed across all projects, and how consistently the two-track design offers comparable coverage within the industries where finals are actually held.

Publication practice deserves the same attention as the prize schedule. If a later report printed only the monetary grades while earlier reports listed excellence recipients, a count of names would suggest a contraction in recognition even if schedules and awards were unchanged. The Shenzhen archive indicates the possible scale: a podium-only extraction would retain 123 of 323 published award entries, and an analyst with only the shortened notices could reconstruct neither the broad rate nor the within-bracket comparisons involving the other 200 winners. A short statement of which grades each notice covers would prevent the error.

sec.title: 5.3. Implications for entrepreneurship research
sec.p: The right treatment date depends on the mechanism. In McKenzie’s experiment (McKenzie, 2017), access to a grant is central; in Howell (2020)’s work, outside audiences learn about a venture from the competition result. Shenzhen’s rules give these accounts different starting points. The award announcement dates public recognition, whereas disbursement would date the receipt of funds. A single winner flag recorded at announcement assigns both events to the same projects on the same day, and the public notices justify only the first.

A study linking these records to later financing also has to choose where to start following projects. Starting at the finalist notice keeps projects that left the final without a distinction; starting at the award announcement selects only winners if that list is all the researcher has. The difference in the risk set is large. In the two complete editions, 132 finalists received no award, 41 enterprises and 91 teams, and all of them would vanish from an award-list sampling frame. Comparisons across grades within such a sample can still be informative, but they answer a question conditional on winning. Reconstructing the full finalist roster keeps the earlier comparison available and documents whom the later starting point excludes.

Even the finalist roster conditions on earlier selection. In 2024, 117 teams qualified for the city industry final and 68 appeared on the award list; in 2025 the figures were 85 and 43. Both comparisons begin after qualifying panels had made their choices. If more teams entered the earlier rounds and faced a stricter filter, the final-round rates would not reveal it. A study of admission would need the application and qualifying lists, each application’s track and the date of the qualifying decision, none of which the final-round prize counts can supply.

Prediction faces a related limit. McKenzie &amp; Sansone (2019) compared judges’ scores with alternative methods for predicting the success of entrants to a Nigerian business plan competition. Moving from a score to a grade loses detail within a single panel; moving from a grade to any award loses more, as the pair comparison shows directly. How much predictive information survives each step can be estimated only with a later outcome and an out-of-sample design. The Shenzhen records do establish one hard limit: in a fully recognized final, broad award status gives every project the same value, and no amount of modelling can restore the ranking removed with the grade.

The method transfers only to programmes with a comparable structure. Accelerators differ in the services they deliver, in how cohorts are organized and in how much discretion founders retain (Cohen et al., 2019a; Cohen et al., 2019b), and the link between participation and performance depends on the institutional setting (Tank et al., 2024; Yagüe-Perales et al., 2024). A city competition with an announced roster and fixed grades lends itself to a comparison of capacity and outcome. A mentoring programme that offers repeated introductions at mentors’ discretion does not, because its units of support are neither fixed in advance nor mutually exclusive. Applying the approach elsewhere requires a definable set of eligible entrants at the relevant decision and a finite allocation that governed it; a shared label such as “entrepreneurship support” is not enough.

Research on Chinese technology markets links regional institutions with entrepreneurial activity (Li et al., 2025), and related work examines venture capital and technology commercialization (Zhang et al., 2024) and the effect of technology finance pilot policies on urban entrepreneurship (Du et al., 2025). Award records could add specific, dated contacts between a local programme and individual projects to this literature, provided their different intensities are kept apart. A public excellence award, eligibility for a monetary prize and a verified transfer of funds are three distinct events. Coding them all as public financial support would obscure both the programme and the firms it reached.

Comparisons across cities face the same problem in sharper form. Two cities could report the same share of finalists with prizes, one awarding money at every grade and the other adding a long list of noncash distinctions below its monetary tiers. Equal overall rates would then say something about how many entrants were publicly named and little about how many could claim payment. Conversely, a study of public endorsement that dropped all noncash prizes would exclude events both cities used deliberately. A defensible comparison starts from the outcome of interest, identifies the local categories that implement it, and only then compares counts. The Shenzhen results show how large the error can be even within a single city.

sec.title: 5.4. Limitations and directions for further research
sec.p: The study follows projects from admission to the municipal final through publication of the results. It does not observe the earlier pool of eligible firms and teams, founders who considered entering, or projects eliminated at district and semifinal stages, so a change in final-round recognition could coexist with an opposite change in earlier selection. Announced finalists are the right denominator for the question asked here, but estimating a founder’s prospects at the point of applying would require entry and advancement records.

The analysis also stops before disbursement and later performance. Claiming a prize may require further action, particularly where a team’s payment depends on local registration. A useful extension would record three dates for each awardee (the announcement, fulfilment of any registration condition, and payment) and link them to later financing. That would separate the timing of public endorsement from the receipt of funds and show which announced prizes were never paid.

The reallocation exercise holds the roster fixed, and this is its main limitation. Evidence from tournaments gives good reason to take incentive effects seriously (Ehrenberg & Bognanno, 1990). If a city that previously offered few team prizes announced many more, some teams might enter that would otherwise have stayed away, enterprises might change the effort they put into a pitch, and qualifying panels might face a different pool. The calculated reallocation would then apply to a roster that no longer exists. Recording when entrants first saw each version of a schedule, together with entries and withdrawals before and after a revision, would allow the entry margin to be studied, and panel scores and submission histories would help to distinguish a change in who competed from a change in how far prizes extended down the ranking.

The evidence is strongest for 2024 and 2025. In 2023 the study records contain the overall team finalist count but not the industry assignments of 23 team finalists, so the first-prize result remained interpretable under every feasible assignment while the adjusted overall difference could change sign. Extending the findings to other cities would require matching the stage of competition, the registration rule, the industries in which finalists were ranked and the point at which a prize carried a financial entitlement.

Finally, the records show selectivity conditional on the published roster, not what outside audiences understood at the time. An entrepreneur might have seen only the award list, or the finalist notice as well. A project named in both had two public appearances even when every finalist in its bracket won, and those appearances carried different information for someone who knew the finalist pool than for someone meeting the project for the first time. Whether and how investors read the grades is an empirical question for future work. The within-bracket evidence provides a starting point: a claim that investors could rank the information technology enterprise finalists by whether each won a prize faces the immediate difficulty that all of them did, whereas a claim that investors attended to grade is consistent with what the lists contain and can be tested against later decisions.

sec.title: 6. Conclusion
sec.p: In Shenzhen’s 2024 and 2025 industry finals, the enterprise advantage depended on how far down the prize list one counted. The two tracks received fourteen first prizes each; adding second prizes put enterprises ahead, and adding excellence awards widened the gap to 28.84 percentage points. The schedule published in advance, capped at each finalist roster, accounts for all 96 observed counts at individual grades. The headline difference between registered firms and entrepreneurial teams is therefore fully consistent with the allocation of places, and a winner flag can stand for quite different events within the same city and edition.

Of the 4,479 pairs of finalists drawn from the same year, industry and track, the published grades distinguish 3,043 and a winner flag only 1,645. Recording whether an award carried a monetary entitlement would recover 1,155 of the 1,398 lost distinctions, provided that noncash excellence recipients remain identifiable alongside unawarded finalists. Organizers can preserve all of these comparisons by publishing grades against the original finalist roster. Researchers following ventures after a competition should code outcomes at least at the level of no award, noncash recognition and cash-bearing prize, and should rely on payment records, not award lists, to establish who actually received money.

notes.title: Data Availability Statement
notes.p: Supplementary Table S1 provides the counts needed to reproduce the track-level award rates and the binary, three-category and full-grade pair totals for 2024 and 2025. The finalist notices, competition plans and award notices are identified in the references. The extraction files, verified record links and the 2023 calculations are available from the corresponding author on request.
